## Definition

For the continuous-function architecture, given a finite partition of $D$ into measurable cells $E_1,\dots,E_N$, choose tags $\xi_j\in E_j$ and weights $\omega_j=|E_j|$. For input samples $v_0(\xi_j)$, replace each integral layer by
$$v_{t+1}^{(i)}=\sigma_t\!\left(W_tv_t^{(i)}+\sum_{j=1}^N\omega_j\kappa_t(\xi_i,\xi_j)v_t^{(j)}+b_t(\xi_i)\right),\qquad 1\le i\le N.$$
At an arbitrary output query $x\in\bar D'$, evaluate the same layer formula using $x$ in the first kernel argument and the stored input-cell values in the sum. Apply the pointwise lifting and projection networks with the same parameters at every discretization. A refinement changes the cells, tags, and weights, but not the continuum parameters $W_t,\kappa_t,b_t$ or the pointwise network parameters.

## Definition

The raw quadrature rule below takes the continuous input function, including any off-grid values used by a local term or pointwise lifting. It is not by itself asserted to factor through its stored input samples. A finite-sampling version is specified after the raw rule.

For the continuous-function architecture, given a finite partition of $D$ into measurable cells $E_1,\dots,E_N$, choose tags $\xi_j\in E_j$ and weights $\omega_j=|E_j|$. For input samples $v_0(\xi_j)$, replace each integral layer by
$$v_{t+1}^{(i)}=\sigma_t\!\left(W_tv_t^{(i)}+\sum_{j=1}^N\omega_j\kappa_t(\xi_i,\xi_j)v_t^{(j)}+b_t(\xi_i)\right),\qquad 1\le i\le N.$$
At an arbitrary output query $x\in\bar D'$, evaluate the same layer formula using $x$ in the first kernel argument and the stored input-cell values in the sum. Apply the pointwise lifting and projection networks with the same parameters at every discretization. A refinement changes the cells, tags, and weights, but not the continuum parameters $W_t,\kappa_t,b_t$ or the pointwise network parameters.

For a finite-sampling realization on continuous inputs, first reconstruct the input from its prescribed tags by the normalized nonnegative weights in the finite-sampling reconstruction bridge. Run the raw rule on this reconstructed function, including in the pointwise lifting and every local term. Its output is then a function of the finite input sample vector alone, with the same continuum parameters. The weights and reconstruction change with the partition; the learned parameters do not. The bridge proves compact-uniform convergence in the output supremum norm. For a stronger compatible Banach input/output formulation, supply reconstructions into the actual input Banach space that converge compact-uniformly in that input norm; the same bridge then preserves the raw rule's proved output Banach norm convergence. The explicit continuous-input weights alone do not assert this stronger reconstruction property.

## Remark

At every refinement, each cell contributes its volume weight, all kernels and pointwise-network parameters are shared with the continuum operator, and the output can be evaluated at any query point. Changing only the mesh size without preserving these three conventions does not instantiate the discretization family defined above.

The integral universality subclass also admits $L^1$ input equivalence classes. Point samples of those classes are not canonical; this algorithm uses continuous representatives when applying sampling and makes no assertion of an intrinsic point-sampling rule on arbitrary $L^1$ classes. Norm convergence of the reconstructions requires the hypotheses of the discretization theorem for the chosen norm.

## Statement

Let a finite neural operator have bounded domains, continuous kernels and biases, continuous pointwise activations, and continuous pointwise lifting and projection networks. For every integral use finite measurable partitions whose cells have tags, volume weights, and maximal diameter tending to zero. Its compatible quadratures converge in the output supremum norm uniformly on every compact input set in $C(\bar D)$, and hence on compact subsets of any Banach input space continuously included in $C(\bar D)$. Intermediate values in these realizations are evaluated by their defining functions at all required tags and output queries; changing meshes does not change the continuum parameters.

More generally, the same conclusion holds in the output Banach norm for the following compatible-space architecture. At each stage choose a Banach function space $X_t$ continuously included in $C(\bar D_t;\mathbb R^{q_t})$. For an integral layer from $X_t$ to an auxiliary Banach function space $Y_t$ of $\mathbb R^{q_{t+1}}$-valued functions on $\bar D_{t+1}$, require a continuous inclusion $Y_t\hookrightarrow C(\bar D_{t+1};\mathbb R^{q_{t+1}})$ and require that $y\mapsto\kappa_t(\cdot,y)$ be continuous from $\bar D_t$ into the space of linear maps $\mathbb R^{q_t}\to Y_t$, in operator norm. Every local linear term is a bounded map $X_t\to Y_t$, its bias belongs to $Y_t$, and its following activation is a continuous map $Y_t\to X_{t+1}$. Any separate lifting and projection maps are continuous between their specified Banach spaces. The same maps are used in the discrete and continuum constructions. No arbitrary output Banach norm follows from its continuous inclusion into the supremum norm alone.

## Proof

1.1 Write $I(v)=\int_D\kappa(\cdot,y)v(y)\,dy$ for one compatible Banach layer, and let $C$ be a compact subset of its input space $X$. Its image in $C(\bar D)$ is compact: pulling an open cover back through the continuous inclusion and using compactness proves this directly. Thus $R=\sup_{v\in C}\|v\|_\infty<\infty$. This family has a common modulus of continuity tending to zero. Indeed a finite $\eta$-net in the supremum norm and uniform continuity of its finitely many functions give $|v(y)-v(z)|\le2\eta+\max_j|v_j(y)-v_j(z)|$ for every $v\in C$. Uniform continuity of the finitely many functions follows by the compact-domain subsequence contradiction. Let $B=\sup_y\|\kappa(\cdot,y)\|_{\mathcal L(\mathbb R^q,Y)}$ and let $\omega_\kappa$ be its norm modulus. Compactness similarly proves $B<\infty$ and $\omega_\kappa(h)\to0$. Therefore the $Y$-valued integrands $\Phi_v(y)=\kappa(\cdot,y)v(y)$ have common modulus bounded by $R\omega_\kappa(h)+B\omega_C(h)$. [given, F1, construct, algebra]

2.1 A continuous $Y$-valued function $\Phi$ on $\bar D$ has an integral in $Y$: volume-weighted step sums on partitions of diameter $h$ form a Cauchy family, since comparing two sums on their common refinement bounds their difference by $|D|\omega_\Phi(h+h')$. Completeness of $Y$ gives a limit, independent of tags and partitions. Each coordinate of point evaluation on $Y$ is bounded by its specified continuous inclusion into $C(\bar D';\mathbb R^{q_{t+1}})$; explicitly, $|u_j(x)|\le c_Y\|u\|_Y$. Applying these bounded functionals to the convergent sums therefore identifies the limit with the pointwise integral in every coordinate. Comparing a fixed tagged sum to refinements and taking the limit gives $\|Q_n(v)-I(v)\|_Y\le |D|[R\omega_\kappa(h_n)+B\omega_C(h_n)]$ uniformly for $v\in C$. Also $\|Q_n(v)-Q_n(w)\|_Y\le |D|B\|v-w\|_\infty\le |D|Bc_X\|v-w\|_X$, where $c_X$ is the embedding bound. These estimates use only measurable disjoint cells, their volumes summing to $|D|$, and their diameter bound. [step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 Suppose inductively that the discrete inputs $v_n(a)$ converge in $X$ to the continuum inputs $v(a)$ uniformly for $a$ in the original compact set $K$. The continuum map is continuous by the bound for $I$ from step 2.1 and continuity of all other maps, so $C=v(K)$ is compact. Comparing preactivations at $v_n(a)$ and $v(a)$, the quadrature Lipschitz bound and the bounded local-map norm give an upper bound $(|D|Bc_X+\|W\|)\|v_n(a)-v(a)\|_X+\|Q_n(v(a))-I(v(a))\|_Y$, which tends to zero uniformly in $a$. The continuum preactivations form a compact set $P\subset Y$. A continuous map $T:Y\to X'$ takes perturbations tending uniformly to zero around $P$ to uniformly vanishing output errors: for a prescribed $\varepsilon$, cover $P$ by finitely many balls $B(p_i,r_i)$ on each of which $\|T(z)-T(p_i)\|<\varepsilon/2$ for $\|z-p_i\|<3r_i$, and use a positive perturbation bound smaller than $\min_i r_i$. If $p\in B(p_i,r_i)$ and $\|z-p\|<\min_i r_i$, both images are within $\varepsilon/2$ of $T(p_i)$. Apply this to the activation. The same argument treats continuous lifting or projection maps. Starting with the identical input and proceeding through the finitely many stages proves uniform convergence in the final Banach norm. [step 2.1, given, construct, algebra]

4.1 For the supremum-norm architecture take every relevant $X$ and $Y$ to be the continuous-function space with its supremum norm. Joint continuity of $\kappa(x,y)$ on the compact product implies continuity of $y\mapsto\kappa(\cdot,y)$ in that norm, by its uniform modulus on the product. Finite matrix local terms are bounded in that norm. For any fixed continuous scalar activation, its induced map on continuous functions is continuous in the supremum norm: near a function of norm $R$, all scalar arguments lie in $[-R-1,R+1]$, where the activation is uniformly continuous. Pointwise finite networks are finite compositions of these continuous maps. Thus all conditions in steps 1.1–2.1 hold, proving the first clause and then its continuously embedded input-space version. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, F1, F2, algebra] ∎

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, $d\ge1$, a compact set $K$, an activation $\sigma$, and—when the $L^p$ clause is used—a finite regular Borel measure $\mu$ with $\mu\ll\lambda_d$, and $1<p<\infty$.

[F1] $\mathcal M$ consists of measurable, locally essentially bounded activations whose discontinuity-set closure is null; $\mathcal M_{\mathrm{pt}}$ additionally requires pointwise local boundedness ([[def-activation-class-locally-essentially-bounded-ae-continuous]]).

[F2] The network family is the scalar finite sum of affine ridge units with an output bias ([[def-single-hidden-layer-network]]).

[F3] Every nonpolynomial-almost-everywhere activation in $\mathcal M_{\mathrm{pt}}$ gives pointwise compact-uniform density ([[lem-rough-nonpolynomial-activation-universal-on-compact-sets]]).

[F4] Real-valued continuous functions restricted from $C_c(\mathbb R^d,\mathbb R)$ are dense in real $L^p(\mu)$ for finite regular compactly supported measures and $1\le p<\infty$ ([[lem-continuous-functions-dense-in-lp-for-compactly-supported-finite-borel-measures]]).

[F5] Nonconstant affine pullbacks of one-dimensional null sets are $d$-dimensional Lebesgue null ([[lem-linear-ridge-pullback-of-null-sets-is-null]]).

[F6] A nonzero real polynomial on $\mathbb R^d$ has a Lebesgue-null zero set ([[lem-nonzero-real-polynomial-zero-set-is-lebesgue-null]]).

[F7] If $\sigma$ is polynomial almost everywhere, single-hidden-layer networks fail uniform density on a compact segment ([[lem-polynomial-activation-bounded-degree-obstruction]]).

[F8] $L^p(\mu)$ identifies functions equal $\mu$-almost everywhere, and $\mu\ll\lambda_d$ means every Lebesgue-null set is $\mu$-null ([[def-calligraphic-l-p-on-a-measure-space]], [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]], [[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]).

[F9] Closed bounded subsets of finite-dimensional Euclidean space are compact ([[thm-heine-borel-rn]]).

[F10] A measure is a nonnegative countably additive set function on a sigma-algebra; since $\mu$ is concentrated on $K$, countable additivity on $K\sqcup(\mathbb R^d\setminus K)$ gives $\mu(\mathbb R^d)=\mu(K)$ ([[def-measure]]).

[F11] For $1\le p\le\infty$, the quotient $L^p(\mu)$ has the norm induced by its integral or essential-supremum functional, and the norm satisfies the triangle inequality ([[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]).

[F12] On a finite measure space, every essentially bounded function belongs to $L^p$ and $\|h\|_p\le\mu(X)^{1/p}\|h\|_\infty$ for $1\le p<\infty$; a pointwise bound $|h|\le M$ on the compact set carrying $\mu$ implies $\|h\|_\infty\le M$ ([[thm-finite-measure-l-r-includes-into-l-p-for-p-less-r]], [[def-essential-supremum-with-respect-to-a-measure]]).

[F13] A continuous real-valued function on a nonempty compact metric space attains its minimum ([[thm-extreme-value-metric]]).

[F14] Every Cauchy sequence of real numbers converges ([[thm-reals-cauchy-complete]]).

[F15] Under Countable Choice, the Lebesgue measure of $[0,1]^d$ is $1$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]]).

[F16] Under Countable Choice, every Lebesgue measurable subset of $\mathbb R$ is an $F_\sigma$ set together with an outer-null set ([[thm-littlewood-characterisations-of-lebesgue-measurability]]).

[F17] Under Countable Choice every Borel subset of $\mathbb R^d$ is Lebesgue measurable ([[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]]).

[F18] Under Countable Choice, for every Lebesgue measurable set $E$ and $\varepsilon>0$ there is a compact $F\subseteq E$ with $\lambda_d(E\setminus F)<\varepsilon$ ([[thm-lebesgue-inner-regularity-by-closed-and-compact-sets]]).

[A1] Countable Choice means every sequence of nonempty sets has a function choosing one element from each ([[def-countable-choice]]).
